new_statements.quote: El acento se escribe como en español. Las palabras que terminan en vocal o en las consonantes n o s tienen el acento en la penúltima sílaba. Las palabras que terminan en una consonante que no sea n o s tienen el acento en la última sílaba. Se escribe el acento cuando es la excepción de la regla. Por ejemplo, no se escribe el acento en las palabras popolucas ma̱šu [má̱šu] manso, camdʉjc [camdʉ́jc] acahual y ma̱yin [má̱yin] pepegua. Pero se escribe en las palabras ámbanu antiguo, cáduts agrio.
new_statements.translation: The accent is written as in Spanish. Words ending in a vowel or in the consonants n or s have the accent on the penultimate syllable. Words ending in a consonant other than n or s have the accent on the last syllable. The accent is written when a word is an exception to the rule. For example, no accent is written on the Popoluca words ma̱šu [má̱šu] 'tame', camdʉjc [camdʉ́jc] 'fallow field' and ma̱yin [má̱yin] 'pepegua'. But it is written on the words ámbanu 'old', cáduts 'sour'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress position is a property of each word that the practical orthography records: by a Spanish-style convention it is left unmarked when it falls on the penult of a vowel-/n-/s-final word or on the final syllable of a word ending in another consonant, and marked with an acute otherwise (exceptions include initial/antepenultimate stress, e.g. ámbanu, cáduts, and in the same notes újtsat 'nosotros', míjchat 'ustedes', jé'jat 'ellos'). The passage gives no phonological or morphological rule predicting stress; it only implies that most words are penult- or final-stressed and that exceptions exist.
new_statements.exceptions: ámbanu 'antiguo', cáduts 'agrio' carry a written accent as exceptions to the default; pronoun plurals újtsat, míjchat, jé'jat (p. 80) are likewise written with accent (stress on the stem rather than the -at plural suffix).
new_statements.domain_note: Orthographic word / dictionary citation forms. This is a spelling convention in a vocabulary's grammar notes, written by the primary describer of the language, not an explicit phonological analysis; Clark's 1969 Tlalocan text marks stress on every word (final, penult and antepenult positions all occur, e.g. yawayná?, igikupé·ga, iyáhkahaw), consistent with stress being lexically/morphologically rather than positionally fixed. Clark 1959 (Studies in Linguistics 14) and the grammatical outline in Clark 1961 should contain the phonological statement and would supersede this.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Popoluca of Sayula de Alemán, Veracruz (sayu1241 itself; Clark's fieldwork from the 1950s onward). No dialect split is at issue.

sources.locator: Notas gramaticales, §1 'Fonología', p. 80 (PDF p. 95 of the SIL facsimile)
sources.note: Notas gramaticales §1 Fonología, p. 80 (PDF p. 95): accent is written as in Spanish -- words ending in a vowel or n/s are stressed on the penult, words ending in any other consonant on the final syllable, and the acute is written only on exceptions (e.g. ámbanu 'antiguo', cáduts 'agrio'; unwritten in ma̱šu [má̱šu], camdʉjc [camdʉ́jc], ma̱yin [má̱yin]). An orthographic default-plus-exceptions statement, not a phonological rule.
Phoneme inventory only; nothing on stress. Bibliography lists Clark 1959, 1961, 1983, 1995.
